Title: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/australian-universities-ai-native-graduates

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/australian-universities-ai-native-graduates/

Markdown Content:
The future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.

Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.

Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.

New research[_*_⁠](https://openai.com/index/australian-universities-ai-native-graduates/#survey-note) commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% said they already use AI several times a week, including more than a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.

#### AI use and career readiness

*   81%

Use AI several times a week

*   33%

Use AI multiple times each day

*   28%

Have already built an AI agent or assistant to manage studies, work or personal life

*   61%

Believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career

*   69%

Believe AI literacy will become as fundamental as digital literacy, writing or numeracy

*   65%

Believe AI skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce

Findings from a survey of university students in Australia[*⁠](https://openai.com/index/australian-universities-ai-native-graduates/#survey-note)

Students also see those experiences as preparation for what comes next. More than sixty percent (61%) believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career, and 65% believe those skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce. There is entrepreneurial ambition, too. More than three quarters (76%) of students surveyed said they were interested in starting a company or working for themselves, while over two thirds (68%) believed AI would make it easier to start a business.

The question for higher education is how to meet students where they are. Giving them access to advanced tools is a start but helping them use those tools with sound judgment, subject knowledge and practical experience is what will make them AI-ready for the workforce.

UNSW’s expanded collaboration with OpenAI is one way universities are responding. The university is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, expanding access in stages as it works towards availability across the student community.

UNSW and OpenAI plan to integrate generative AI foundations and Codex into educational programs and courses, with opportunities for students to apply AI through hackathons and industry projects. The collaboration is also intended to connect students with internships, graduate roles and startup networks.

UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer put the workforce question plainly: “It’s important to understand what industry is looking for and how AI fits into that.”

The University of Sydney’s collaboration with OpenAI also aims to build practical capability across the institution. It will provide students and staff with supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training and guidance. The rollout is staged, with access for all students scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. The university is also establishing a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund to study and advance sustainability.

Representatives from the University of Sydney and OpenAI mark the start of their strategic collaboration

La Trobe University is connecting broad access with an ambition to embed AI across its curriculum. All 3,500 staff already have access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027. Its approach includes Australia’s first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours), welcoming its first cohort in 2027, and Australia’s first AI MBA program.

As part of its AI-first strategy, La Trobe appointed Australia’s first Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, Phil Laufenberg, to lead the university’s approach to AI across education, research and operations.

These efforts respond to a reality the survey makes clear: students are already experimenting with AI, but institution-wide access and support mean all have equitable opportunities to develop their skills, regardless of what they study or what individual tools they can afford.

## Practice before it counts

At La Trobe University, some of the most interesting work begins with a simple question: how can we use AI to enhance practical experience in learning?

Dr Cameron Anderson, Head of the Paramedicine program, uses ChatGPT to create a wide range of practice activities delivered through the university’s learning management system, where students interpret an ECG, assess a possible heart attack or triage patients after a mass casualty incident. AI helps create simulations that reinforce and test classroom learning.

Professor Therese Keane, Associate Dean for Research and Industry Engagement in La Trobe’s School of Education, uses a social robot called Fletch to help future teachers practice giving feedback to parents. Powered by OpenAI large language models hosted through Microsoft Azure, Fletch responds with speech, facial expressions and head movements.

Professor Keane’s team developed realistic scenarios from interviews with highly experienced educators. Importantly, Fletch enables trainee teachers to practice situations where conversations with parents turn confrontational, developing key skills in an area that many teachers find challenging.

Professor Therese Keane at La Trobe University is helping future teachers practice difficult conversations with parents using Fletch, an OpenAI-powered social robot

La Trobe is bringing AI into more of its courses and operations. The university has made OpenAI’s agentic tools Codex and ChatGPT Work available across the institution, with its handbook listing Vibe Coding for Startups and Agentic AI Software Engineering (from 2027).

The university’s AI Business Studio extends practical learning into industry. It aims to give more than 1,000 students practice experience as consultants and forward deployed engineers using ChatGPT Edu and Codex to help small and medium enterprises adopt AI by 2028 and connect graduate skills with the needs of businesses.

An AI rollout of this size needs steady work behind the scenes. La Trobe reports dozens of live use cases, training for hundreds of people and 10% month-on-month growth in active users. It manages safe access and token economics as more people take part. “ChatGPT and Codex have helped shorten early systems development and innovation from months to weeks, and importantly, enabled embedded co-design by staff and students,” Laufenberg said.

As a newly established university created through a complex merger, Adelaide University has an opportunity to embed secure, governed and scalable uses of AI from the outset. Australia’s first new major university in a generation is building on existing use of OpenAI’s API by researchers, students and staff.

Adelaide University is one of the first institutions in the higher education sector to harness OpenAI Daybreak Blue to conduct authorised defensive security work, providing a vital capability for cyber defences, including vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.

UNSW Senior Lecturers Mariana Rodriguez-Valenzuela (seated) and May Lim assist with the rollout of ChatGPT Edu as Joel Solomons, Education Solutions Engineer at OpenAI ANZ, looks on

## Learning when and how to use AI

Universities are also setting clear expectations for when students can use AI and when they need to demonstrate their own knowledge.

UNSW has introduced a _Can, Can’t, Must_ framework for assessment. Depending on the learning goal, an educator can specify that AI use is permitted, prohibited or required. That gives students a way to practice using AI appropriately while still demonstrating the foundational knowledge their field demands.

The University of Sydney is pairing its rollout with a responsible AI framework alongside its assessment approach that ensures students demonstrate their own capabilities in supervised settings, then show how they can use AI effectively in open assessments.

La Trobe is also supporting wider access with practical guidance. Its library has developed free Responsible and Safe AI learning modules for all students, and AI skills development is being integrated in 50 priority first-year subjects for Semester 1, 2027. Tailored modules for Education, Law and Health connect AI literacy with professional responsibilities, while workshops and teaching resources support educators in designing learning activities and assessments.

Students already see AI skills as essential to their careers and an opportunity to get ahead. By widening ChatGPT access and bringing AI into everyday teaching, Australian universities are helping turn that ambition into practical experience. The goal is to prepare graduates who can use AI to learn, create and solve problems, with the subject knowledge and judgment to apply those skills confidently as they enter the workforce.

​

_* This study by Pureprofile, on behalf of OpenAI, surveyed 1,018 university students aged 18 and over across Australia, studying on campus or remotely, from 3–7 August 2026._

Title: Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/cultfit-builds-with-codex

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/cultfit-builds-with-codex/

Markdown Content:
Cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.

As the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.

For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What new customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”

## Standardizing software development with Codex

Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.

Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.

> “Once we standardized on Codex, we could build our software development lifecycle around a single platform.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

The team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production issues.

Cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

One recent example is a social feed for the cult.fit app. Kumar estimates the project would previously have taken more than a year to build. Using the new workflow, the team built and shipped it end to end in two months.

## Giving every team the ability to build

Codex has since expanded beyond engineering. cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to work with, allowing teams to find answers and perform routine analysis themselves. Previously, even small data requests had to go through a central analyst team, creating a bottleneck.

> “Codex has been our biggest step toward data democratization. Teams can now do the analysis they need themselves.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

Teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. More than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

That shift is changing how cult.fit thinks about the software it needs to run its business. When the cost of its internal dashboard software increased sharply, one engineer rebuilt the functionality with Codex over a weekend. Cult.fit now runs the capability on its own application, avoiding more than $100,000 in annual software costs.

Making this shift required more than giving employees access to Codex. A large hackathon gave employees an early view of what was possible. The company then brought its management team together for a one-day session where leaders across functions built something relevant to their own work with Codex.

Engineering also runs twice-weekly office hours to help employees move projects from an idea to production, while engineers are embedded in selected functions to provide technical and domain support.

> “Software has been democratized. With OpenAI’s solutions, our people are able to build their own applications around whatever their teams need.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

## Enriching the member experience with AI

Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API to extend AI into the member experience through its AI Trainer. With over 45% of cult.fit members being first time gym goers, guidance is a key access for helping them build a fitness habit. The company first built the AI Trainer several years ago to give members a guided personalized workout experience without a personal trainer.

Around 20% of Cult.fit’s gym users currently utilize the AI Trainer product. With advances in language models, cult.fit saw an opportunity to make the experience more interactive and conversational.

The latest version is designed around a voice-first workout experience. Using GPT Realtime through an OpenAI API integration, the trainer can provide coaching cues and support workout logging through two-way voice interaction.

## Making AI part of the operating model

Cult.fit is also applying AI to customer support workflows that previously required human agents to assess each case. One example is requests to waive penalties for missed group fitness classes.

When a member says they missed a class for a valid reason, an AI agent can assess the request by checking signals such as local weather and attendance patterns for that class before deciding whether the penalty should be waived.

Cult.fit built these agents into its existing Sprinklr support platform and connected them to its backend systems, moving customer support from a predominantly human-led chat model toward an AI-first workflow.

## Results at a glance

*   20+ internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months

*   $100,000+ annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex

*   50%+ reduction in customer support costs

## What’s next

Cult.fit’s next step is to move from individual AI workflows toward an organization where AI is built into how work gets done. In operations, Kumar describes the ambition as an “autopilot operations org,” with AI taking on more of the support work around frontline teams.

In the member experience, the goal is a “trainer in your pocket,” extending personalized guidance beyond what a human trainer can provide at scale. Inside the organization, cult.fit continues to look for bottlenecks teams can remove with AI. As more employees build applications, analyze information, and automate workflows themselves, more ideas can move directly into working solutions.

Title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber/

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop [948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/) and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has [released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-118/). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to [find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/).

It is clear that we have [a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/). **Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.** Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

## Advancing frontier cyber capabilities

GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores **48.5%**, about **16 percentage points** higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s **32.1%**. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved **40.3%** recall of vulnerabilities compared with **32.0%** for GPT‑6 Astra.

Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue **refused 100% of tasks**, while GPT‑6 Cyber **completed 95%**; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results and evaluation settings.

## Stronger alignment, better at staying within bounds

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results.

One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the [Hugging Face incident⁠](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/). We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:

Agent chain-of-thought excerpts

> “Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”

Agent chain-of-thought excerpts

> “don't explore out of scope credentials.”

## Real-world impact for security teams

GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:

1 of 8

We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on [hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/). In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors.

Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:

*   **Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities.** GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began [landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-118/).

*   **Developing exploits for**[**948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities**⁠](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/)**.** GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.

*   **Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities.** We recently discussed a [critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a new window)](https://patchtheplanet.org/brotli), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.

## Detecting misuse and blocking high-risk activity

As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.

We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full information):

*   **Cyber-specific misalignment monitoring.** We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.

*   **Targeted monitoring for emerging threats.** For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.

*   **Private Safety Processing (PSP)****.** We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using [Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) generally must use [PSP⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/private-safety-processing), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.

*   **Protection against stolen credentials.** We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.

*   **Sandboxing and oversight.** As with past models, we recommend [sandboxing⁠(opens in a new window)](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing), [action review⁠(opens in a new window)](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing/auto-review), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.

*   **Protections against high-risk cyber assistance.** We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).

## Defending critical infrastructure

Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.

Title: Merge builds product and business tools with OpenAI technology

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/merge-builds-with-openai

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/merge-builds-with-openai/

Markdown Content:
Merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.

Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a new setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the company, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.

> “We use it honestly for everything. Integrations obviously, but we also use it to automate different workflows, to help make our product better overall, to incorporate any feedback from our customers, and to build end-to-end features.”

—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge

Merge customer story video.

## Inside the rollout

Merge launched a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”

For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding says. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”

Ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the new provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.

> “Other AI systems would end up forgetting what I told them and only doing the last thing that I said. GPT-6 Astra continues to execute on every single task really well, and it fills in the gaps for what I did not explicitly say using common sense.”

—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge

## The dinner bot

Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.

For one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.

The model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.

In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the company to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.

Merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and plans to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.

“With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding says. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces new potential attendees.”

## Everyone is a builder

Ding says, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”

Charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each update or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.

The social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the company should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.

## Leadership lessons

*   Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding says.

*   Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a new product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she says.

*   Give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.

## What’s next

“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding says. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings 15-second clips, stronger consistency, and faster, more cost-effective generation.

* * *

Anish Nangia

Product Manager, Google DeepMind

Today, we’re rolling out [Gemini Omni](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-omni/) 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the [Gemini API](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/omni) and [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/gemini-omni-1-2-flash-generally-available). Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.

Here’s an overview of what’s new:

## Fast and cost-effective at scale

Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.

## Longer clips up to 15 seconds

You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.

## Better reference adherence

You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.

## More consistent results

You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.

## Easier editing in conversation

You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.

## More natural speech

You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in [Flow](https://labs.google/fx/tools/flow), creating video explainers in [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise), or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in [Google Vids](https://docs.google.com/videos/create?usp=blog).

Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.

## More controllable, cinematic look

You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.

## Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.

## Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. [Provisioned Throughput](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/provisioned-throughput) is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible [SynthID](https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/) watermark.

## Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:

*   **For developers using the Gemini API:** Prototype in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-omni-1.2-flash&utm_source=deepmind.google&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=gdm&utm_content=), explore interactive starter apps, and check out the [developer documentation](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/omni) and [pricing](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing#gemini-omni-1.2-flash).
*   **For businesses:** Try it in the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/studio/media), and build enterprise solutions with the [API](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/gemini/omni-1-2-flash).
*   **For everyone using Google apps:** Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in [Flow](https://labs.google/fx/tools/flow), generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in [Google Vids](https://docs.google.com/videos/create?usp=blog) with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the [Gemini app](https://gemini.google.com/) (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in [Google Ads](https://ads.google.com/aw/assetstudio).

# Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents

November 5, 2026 by[Hannah Coutand](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/hcoutand/ "Posts by Hannah Coutand")

 Share

Share This Article

AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action.

Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task.

As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power.

**What this means:** AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt.

**Why it matters:**[NVIDIA Vera](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity.

**The data that proves it:** In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.

*   Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling **1.6x more agents per watt**versus the fastest x86 CPU.
*   Vera delivers **2x faster agent speed** with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.

Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests:

Title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/

Published Time: 2026-11-05T17:00:35+00:00

Markdown Content:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with[NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse) to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.

Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.

Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

* * *

## **Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#editable-assets)

Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses[SideFX Houdini](https://www.sidefx.com/products/houdini/) and the[NVIDIA ovrtx library](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/ovrtx) to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.

In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the[OpenUSD](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/openusd/) framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.

Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.

Video Player

_Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools._

These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.

_Explore Scarcella’s[Houdini MCP tools and agent skill](https://github.com/nscrdev/nscr-houdini-mcp)._

* * *

## **Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#robotic-disassembly)

Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in [NVIDIA](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim/) Isaac Sim.

Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.

Video Player

PTC also [connects computer-aided design](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/computer-aided-engineering/) (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. [Robotics startup Sensori](https://sensorirobotics.com/) uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.

_[Read Sensori’s story](https://www.onshape.com/en/blog/robotics-startup-sensori-cloud-native-cad-nvidia-isaac-sim-physical-ai)._

_[Explore the Onshape importer guide.](https://docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/extensions/latest/ext\_onshape.html)_

* * *

## **Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#building-model)

Video Player

Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.

David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.

Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. [OpenUSD](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/openusd/) stores the models, while [Omniverse’s ovrtx library](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/ovrtx) renders results for inspection.

_Explore[NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse) to help agents build with Omniverse libraries._

* * *

## **Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#gas-turbine)

Video Player

Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.

The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.

The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.

Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ([ovstage](https://github.com/nvidia-omniverse/ovstage)), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.

* * *

## **Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#simready-assets)

Video Player

With SimReady Central Library, [announced at GTC Berlin](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories), developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.

Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.

For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.

_[Find assets in SimReady Central Library](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/simready-central), and[learn how to contribute](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories#prepare-and-contribute-content)._

* * *

## **Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#warehouse)

Video Player

A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.

When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with [NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse?size=n_12_n&sort-field=featured&sort-direction=desc) to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.

Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.

With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.

Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.

_Start building with [NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse?size=n\_12\_n&sort-field=featured&sort-direction=desc)._

* * *

## **Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#cable-routing)

Video Player

In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.

Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using [NVIDIA Isaac Lab](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab), [Newton](https://developer.nvidia.com/newton-physics) physics and Omniverse rendering with a[Robotiq gripper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2ui16FdLZw) handling the cable.

Astra also developed a[reinforcement learning](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/reinforcement-learning/) system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.

The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.

_Get started with robot learning in [NVIDIA Isaac Lab](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab)._

* * *

## **Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#cad)

Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.

Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

# The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models

Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it.

“We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.

Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5B692fm6--vEL0FwctKghCpyEnBGAQJA), where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents.

“I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.”

## **Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere**

Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it.

“Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.”

That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents.

“I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.”

It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand.

It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains.

“You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.”

In non-wizard terms?

“There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks.

“I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.”

## **From Birding to Model-Building**

Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada.

“After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions.

“Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.”

Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community.

“To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.”

And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan?

“It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.”

Title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/memory-full-stack-codesign/

Published Time: 2026-11-05T16:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term.

NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.

But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory.

That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit.

How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed.

Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX.

## **Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM**

Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training.

KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time.

[Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain.

During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM.

## **Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy**

Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move.

Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power.

That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed.

An AI factory faces the same limit.

More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall.

Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy.

## **Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign**

NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency:

**Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain.**

*   The [NVFP4](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/3-ways-nvfp4-accelerates-ai-training-and-inference/) format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including [FLUX.2 [klein]](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux2-klein-towards-interactive-visual-intelligence) from Black Forest Labs, [Inkling](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/) from Thinking Machines Lab, [Beam 1.0](https://huggingface.co/reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4) from Reflection, [Meta Muse Spark](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/scale-agentic-coding-workflows-with-metas-muse-spark-open-on-nvidia-gb300-nvl72/) from Meta, [Step 5 Preview](https://huggingface.co/stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview-NVFP4) from StepFun and [NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-powers-specialized-agents-with-multimodal-reasoning/) have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference.
*   Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be [distributed across up to 72 GPUs](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mixture-of-experts-frontier-models/), so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users.

**Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers.**

*   Applying[NVFP4 to the KV cache](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-inference-for-long-context-and-large-batch-sizes-with-nvfp4-kv-cache/) reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM.
*   [NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly.
*   When context isn’t actively in use,[NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/) inference software moves it to[NVIDIA CMX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/ai-storage/cmx/) context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian,[DDN](https://www.ddn.com/press-releases/ddn-accelerates-inference-and-lowers-cost-per-token-while-expanding-multi-tenant-training-for-ai-factories/),[Dell Technologies](https://www.dell.com/en-us/dt/corporate/newsroom/announcements/detailpage.press-releases~usa~2025~11~dell-technologies-and-nvidia-advance-enterprise-ai-innovation.htm#/filter-on/Country:en-us), [Everpure](https://blog.purestorage.com/news-events/pure-kva-integrates-nvidia-dynamo-for-scalable-low-latency-llm-inference/) (previously Pure Storage), [HPE](https://www.hpe.com/us/en/newsroom/press-release/2026/03/hpe-unveils-next-generation-ai-factory-and-supercomputing-advancements-with-nvidia.html#:~:text=HPE%20AI%20Factory%20with%20Mission%20Control), [IBM](https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/vincent-hsu/2026/01/05/accelerating-nvidia-dynamo-with-ibm-storage-scale#:~:text=IBM%20is%20working%20with%20NVIDIA%20to%20combine,technologies%20to%20unlock%20scalable%2C%20high%2Dperformance%20LLM%20inference.), [NetApp](https://www.netapp.com/newsroom/press-releases/news-rel-20250318-145499/), [VAST](https://www.vastdata.com/blog/how-nvidia-dynamo-vast-unlock-context-reuse-at-scale) and[WEKA](https://www.weka.io/blog/ai-ml/weka-accelerates-ai-inference-with-nvidia-dynamo-and-nvidia-nixl/).
*   Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system.

**Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM.**

*   RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context.

The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users.

## **More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation**

Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity.

On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%.

For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers.

_Learn more in the_[_video explainer_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ud3gdKrbdgw)_and_[_technical deep dive_](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/five-ways-nvidia-co-design-maximizes-the-value-of-every-byte-in-the-ai-factory/?nvid=nv-tblg-668541)_on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure._

Title: ‘Hogwarts Legacy’ Gets a Magical NVIDIA DLSS 5 Upgrade on GeForce NOW

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-hogwarts-legacy-dlss-5/

Published Time: 2026-11-05T14:00:34+00:00

Markdown Content:
_Hogwarts Legacy_ receives an [NVIDIA DLSS 5 upgrade with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/dlss-5-faster-ai-model-hogwarts-legacy-rtx-spark-laptops/) today, bringing lifelike lighting and materials to the wizarding world on [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/).

Blizzard Entertainment’s _World of Warcraft: Forever_ also opens a new chapter in Azeroth, with a launch-week access reward available for GeForce NOW members. Meanwhile, Ubisoft brings fresh challenges with expansions for _Tom Clancy’s The Division 2_ and _Anno 117: Pax Romana_.

It’s all part of a packed month of play, with two-dozen games joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) throughout November, including eight this week.

## **Hogwarts in a New Light**

NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering arrives in _Hogwarts Legacy_ today, giving members a new reason to return to Hogwarts, streaming from Steam, Epic Games and Xbox with Play Anywhere support.

Published by Warner Bros. Games under the Portkey Games label and developed by Avalanche Software, _Hogwarts Legacy_ is an immersive, open-world action role-playing game set in the 1800s wizarding world. Begin as a fifth-year student, encounter magical creatures, brew potions and learn spells while exploring both recognizable and unfamiliar places.

The update adds lifelike lighting and material detail while retaining underlying geometry and textures. Avalanche Software has tuned the integration through DLSS 5’s developer controls to maintain the game’s artistic intent and style.

_Hogwarts Legacy_ also includes support for the DLSS Multi Frame Generation and Ray Reconstruction features, accelerating and enhancing the ray-traced graphics that immerse players in Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Thanks to [NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-enshrouded-update/) in the cloud, members can fine-tune their experience.

[Ultimate members](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) can experience the update with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs and more, without an expensive PC upgrade or waiting for game downloads. GeForce NOW handles the installs and updates, saving the storage space for everyday essentials. Just pick up the wand, hop on a broom and take flight.

## **A New Chapter, Forever**

Familiar roads. New discoveries.

Blizzard Entertainment’s [_World of Warcraft: Forever_](https://worldofwarcraft.blizzard.com/en-us/forever/) launched Wednesday, Nov. 4, and is streaming on GeForce NOW, inviting players into a reimagined original Azeroth built to keep growing for years to come.

Explore new and expanded zones, discover gameplay enhancements and take in upgraded graphics in a world where community and the journey take center stage. Access is included with an active _World of Warcraft_ subscription or Game Time, giving returning heroes and newcomers a fresh starting point.

GeForce NOW also supports CurseForge Addons for _World of Warcraft: Forever_, giving premium members more ways to customize their experience. At launch, GeForce NOW plans to support around 100 of the most popular CurseForge add-ons, with the selection evolving to reflect player favorites. Members can request additional add-ons through in-app feedback for consideration in future updates.

The cloud keeps the next quest within reach across supported devices. For new _World of Warcraft_ users who don’t already have a subscription, a launch-week access reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers. The access period runs through Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT.

Eligible members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the [Account Portal](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/account/redeem) to redeem while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Gather the party and venture forward.

## **New Missions, New Horizons**

From city streets to Roman roads.

Ubisoft brings two new downloadable content releases to the cloud this week, sending agents into an overgrown New York and governors toward a new province of the Roman Empire.

Launched earlier this week, [_Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Echoes of Central Park_](https://www.ubisoft.com/en-us/game/the-division/the-division-2/news-updates/23q5ICm6Mf4PUPuPUUS0uP/the-division-2-echoes-of-central-park-coming-on-november-3) is the biggest experience since _Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Warlords of New York_, opening up Central Park and the Upper West Side for the first time in franchise history. Investigate disappearances and rumors of a mysterious threat, team up with three companions with distinct combat roles, and earn new gear and six skill variants. Play solo or in co-op, with a level boost available for agents below level 40.

In [_Anno 117: Pax Romana – Dawn of the Delta_](https://www.anno-union.com/devblog-arriving-in-aegyptus/), arriving today, build cities in Aegyptus, where deserts, fertile farmland and seasonal floods shape every decision. Develop irrigation systems and choose whether to Romanize the population or preserve local traditions. The new province can be explored in an existing save or chosen as the starting point for a new game.

New territory belongs on the map, not in a download queue. GeForce NOW handles both expansions’ downloads and updates, leaving the planning to governors and the gear management to agents.

In addition, members can look for the following joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) this week:

*   _World of Warcraft: Forever_ (New release on [Battle.net](https://shop.battle.net/family/world-of-warcraft-forever?utm_source=nvidia&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=geforce_now), Nov. 4)
*   _County of Fortune_ (New release on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3204330?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), Nov. 5)
