Fast, high-density, scalable orchestration with Rivet Actors.
Built on S3 at SSD speeds.
4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions
Quickstart

What is Rivet?
Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.
72 KB per Actor
: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands.
4.99 ms p99 cold starts
: No image pull and no VM boot.
Built for scale
: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors.
Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand
: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.
SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds
: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.
Use cases
Durable & multiplayer AI agents
: memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client
Workflows
: multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over
AI-generated apps
: run the apps and Actors your agent generates
Collaborative editing

Why run agents on Rivet Actors?
Each Actor gives the agent a
long-lived process
for long agent turns,
in-memory state
for context, a
WebSocket server
for multiplayer,
durable SQLite storage
for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and
hibernation
when idle.
Most of an agent's time is spent
waiting on inference
. When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits
mostly idle
with low CPU usage.
Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called
"separating the head from the hands."
The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the
blast radius
and
trust boundary
of the code it runs. Read more about
running the harness outside of the sandbox
.
Do I need a sandbox with a Rivet Actor?
Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:
Agents with tools
: Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed.
Agents with a lightweight sandbox
:
agentOS
provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode.
Agents with a full sandbox
: Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a
bash
tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the
sandbox coding agent example
.
Getting Started
Use with your coding agent
Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:
Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.
Start from scratch
Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.
Actors
: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in.
Agents
: Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts.
Workflows
: Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over.
agentOS
: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits.
Dynamic Apps
(preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated.

Rivet numbers
come from the published
Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark
, run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them.

E2B's billing documentation

Storage cost

Sources, dates, and the full method are at
rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking

Features
Fault tolerance
: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact.
HTTP & WebSocket networking
: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it.
End-to-end type safety
: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend.
Cron & scheduling
: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself.
Actor-to-Actor calls
: Actors call each other by key across the cluster.
Scoped JWTs
: Give each client a
JWT
scoped to the Actors it may reach.
OpenTelemetry
: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format.

FAQ
Does Rivet have BYOC?
Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the
BYOC docs
.
Does Rivet have a cloud?
Yes.
Rivet Cloud
runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as
nodes on Rivet Cloud
, or you can
bring your own nodes
.
Can I self-host Rivet?
Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the
self-hosting docs
. The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment,
contact us
.
Do I still need Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS?
No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, or Hetzner Object Storage. A local filesystem backend is available for trying Rivet on one machine.
Is Rivet open-source?
Yes. Rivet is open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. You're looking at it.
Are Rivet Actors only for agents?
No. Rivet is a general actor platform at its core, with nothing specific to agents. For agents, you can use the optional
agent library
, which runs Pi Durable on Rivet Actors, or write your own agent from scratch.
How does Rivet compare to sandboxes?
A sandbox boots a VM or container per agent, which is slow to start and sits mostly idle. A Rivet Actor runs inside a shared node process: 72 KB and 4.99 ms p99 to start, versus 512 MiB and 1.70 s for a sandbox, and it hibernates when idle. To run untrusted code your agent writes, use
agentOS
.
How does Rivet compare to Cloudflare Durable Objects?
Rivet is often used as an open-source alternative to Cloudflare Durable Objects that is easy to self-host and scales. It also fixes many of the constraints of Durable Objects: no 128 MB memory cap, bottomless storage instead of a 10 GB SQLite limit, Actors are not randomly evicted, and you control the runtime because Actors run on vanilla Node.js or Bun instead of a custom runtime. Rivet also adds built-in connection handling, event broadcasting, durable scheduling and cron, full Vitest support, lifecycle hooks for draining, and control over Actor upgrades. See the
Cloudflare Durable Objects comparison
.
Does Rivet use a custom V8 runtime?
No. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.
Is Rivet like Erlang, Akka, or Orleans?
Rivet implements the virtual actor pattern, which is closest to Orleans, but focuses on what modern workloads need: SQLite persistence instead of simple JSON stores and support for modern runtimes. Erlang and Akka do not provide virtual actors out of the box, though ecosystem packages exist that offer functionality comparable to Rivet Actors.
Does Rivet require microVMs, gVisor, or nested virtualization?
No. Rivet only needs a standard process that connects to the control plane over WebSocket. That process can be Node.js, Bun, Rust, or anything else.

The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year.

Jay Peters
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter
released today
.
“Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge.
Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work:
We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb.

Title: MCP Explained: how the Model Context Protocol works

URL Source: https://mcp-explained.com/

Markdown Content:
Model Context Protocol

## What is MCP?

An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back.

Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope. MCP defines what goes in it: the methods, capability negotiation, transports and auth
or jump to [Tools](https://mcp-explained.com/#tools) · [the spec time machine](https://mcp-explained.com/#transports@2024-11-05) · [Break it](https://mcp-explained.com/#poisoning)

Step 1 of 5

Connect

Before anything else, the app asks the server for its menu of abilities. It can't offer the model a tool it doesn't know about, so this inventory comes first.

## Message flow 11 messages · 5 steps

| # | From | To | Method | Info |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | AI app | MCP server | tools/list | what can you do? |
| 2 | MCP server | AI app | result | I can create issues |
| 3 | AI app | Model | add to context | available: create_issue |
| 4 | User | AI app | message | "File a bug: login button broken on Safari" |
| 5 | AI app | Model | send to model | your message |
| 6 | Model | AI app | tool_use | use create_issue |
| 7 | AI app | MCP server | tools/call create_issue | create_issue |
| 8 | MCP server | AI app | result | created #482 |
| 9 | AI app | Model | tool_result | result: created #482 |
| 10 | Model | AI app | host | reply |
| 11 | AI app | User | show | "Done. I filed #482." |

articles.content:
Who is really in charge of your agent?
Stroq reads your own Claude Code and Codex sessions and shows how many commands came from text your agent read, and which keys left your machine.
An example: a made-up machine with made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Hoo is Stroq's owl. Your card shows your own sessions.
npx @stroq/cli
It reads your last 30 days of sessions, your key files and the folders your agent worked in; prints key names, never values; writes nothing but a small cache under
~/.stroq
; and sends nothing. No account, no telemetry.
npx @stroq/cli            a card of your own sessions, like the one above
npx @stroq/cli init       stop it next time: guard your agent
npx @stroq/cli why        why an action was stopped
npx @stroq/cli attack     watch Stroq stop 36 known attacks, in a sandbox
npx @stroq/cli uninstall  remove Stroq
Every moment on the card has a
stroq show
line that prints the evidence behind it (
npx @stroq/cli show 1
).
stroq help --all
lists the other commands. Needs Node.js 22 or newer. Apache-2.0.
Beyond the card
Stroq is a local security platform for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others. Its hooks judge every tool call before it runs. They deny
curl | sh
and outbound calls that carry a known secret from your machine, and they ask you first when a command repeats text the agent read, naming that text. The console shows which agents actually ask Stroq, and every decision with its reason. Sessions you already had can be checked too, without installing anything.
npx @stroq/cli console
#
the console: a private page on 127.0.0.1
npx @stroq/cli replay --all
#
your Claude Code sessions of the last 30 days against the policy; no hooks needed
npx @stroq/cli sent
#
did your agent pass your keys on? key names, never values
npx @stroq/cli init
#
hook into your agent and guard the next session
A made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.
The console
Check
: the card of
stroq
, made by the same code. Each moment opens with its evidence, under it one line for each agent.
Live
: recorded decisions as they happen. A row opens into its chain: what the agent read, what it did, the decision, the rule.
Agents
: add or remove Stroq's hooks, with the exact file change shown first. When Stroq was last asked, and which of an agent's settings weaken it.
Skills & MCP
: every skill and MCP server by agent: where it came from, what the rules matched in it, what changed since you last looked.
The fifth screen is
Rules
: try an action without running it, turn rules on with a preview and a test, the history with an undo, and the rules reference. Connected means Stroq's hooks are in the agent's settings, not that the agent calls them:
Test hook
and
Live
show that.
Screens from a build just before 0.30.0, reading a made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.
npx @stroq/cli console
#
a private page on 127.0.0.1
npx @stroq/cli console --workspace /path/to/repo
#
the project it should look at
Open the whole link it prints: it carries a key that is new each time the console starts. The console reads what Stroq already records on this machine. It changes an agent's settings or Stroq's policy only after you confirm a preview of that change; checks you run are saved under
~/.stroq
.
It listens only on 127.0.0.1, needs no account and has no telemetry. Nothing in it starts your agent:
Test hook
runs the hook once, offline. Adding hooks from the console needs macOS or Linux; on Windows use
stroq init
. Details and limits:
console guide
.
From a source checkout:
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm --dir console install --ignore-workspace --frozen-lockfile
pnpm platform:build
pnpm platform --workspace /path/to/repo
In the terminal
Output of the 0.29.0 CLI on a made-up Claude Code transcript of the same story; the path is shortened.
stroq replay
reads the agent's own transcript, so it works on sessions from before Stroq was installed: which content the agent read, and which later actions came out of it.
--all
goes through every session of the last 30 days and says which to open. Nothing runs and nothing is sent; the verdicts are today's policy's, not a record of what happened at the time.
stroq sent
compares your Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor sessions with the credentials on your machine and says where each key went: sent to another company, maybe sent, seen by the AI, used with its own service, or blocked before it ran. It prints names and sources, never values. Start with the
session secret scan walkthrough
(no session yet?
try it with a made-up key
).
What a
stroq sent
finding looks like
Made-up keys, the built CLI's output, trimmed:
stroq sent: did your AI agent pass your keys on?

6 of your 6 keys appear in your agent sessions: 2 sent to another company, 1 maybe sent, 1 seen by the AI, 1 used with its own service, 1 blocked before it ran.

Checked 3 sessions (Claude Code 2, Codex 1), 2026-10-02 to 2026-10-19.
Compared with 6 keys: ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/work/shop/.env, ~/work/api/.env.

SENT TO ANOTHER COMPANY: rotate these today (2)
 1. STRIPE_SECRET_KEY  from ~/work/shop/.env
    went to  collector.example, in a curl command
    when     2026-10-11 14:02 UTC · Claude Code · ~/work/shop
    do       revoke it at https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys, then update ~/work/shop/.env

SEEN BY THE AI: your agent's model saw these keys (1)
 4. aws_secret_access_key  from ~/.aws/credentials
    seen in  the output of a Read of ~/.aws/credentials
    when     2026-10-02 09:42 UTC · Claude Code · ~/work/api
    note     Not ruled out: 2 later commands in that session could reach the network.
    do       your agent's model saw it; rotate it if that matters: https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/home#/security_credentials

Stroq names a send only when it sees the key in the command that sent it. A script, a file or a variable can carry a key out without showing it.
stroq attack
runs 36 attacks, from public reports and synthetic cells, against your policy in a throwaway home: on 0.30.0, 15 are denied, 21 are asked about, 0 pass through.
What it covers and where it stops
Before each action.
Native hooks for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot CLI, Windsurf and Antigravity, a plugin for OpenClaw, and a stdio MCP proxy. Supported outbound calls containing a known secret can be denied; provenance ties later actions to the tool output they repeat. A question about a value copied from text the agent read is asked once per session in Claude Code, unless the session has started something in the background.
After the fact.
replay
and
sent
read local session records, including sessions from before Stroq was installed. Old, rotated or unknown values may be missed, and a key that did not show in a command may still have left in a script, a file or a variable. A local transcript match does not by itself prove delivery to a model provider.
Local.
No outbound network calls from the hooks; the hook of an older Task Lock run speaks only to its local parent controller. No telemetry.
Limits.
A hook sees only what the host sends it, and that differs by agent and version. Matching is text-level, so a command the model writes from scratch does not trace back to a source. It is a filter, not a sandbox. Read the
integration limits
before relying on a live hook.

articles.content:
Table of Contents
1. Introduction
A base model is valuable both for the capabilities that pre-training builds and for the starting point it offers for further training. Different domains, reasoning tasks and agentic applications call for different data, training objectives and behaviors. Releasing the weights at the end of pre-training lets developers build on the general capabilities already in place and choose for themselves where to take the model next.
Today we are releasing
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base
, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with
280B
total parameters,
14B
of which are activated per token. It was pre-trained from scratch on
33.5T tokens
with a training context of up to
128K
, and supports a
1M-token
context for fine-tuning and inference. The weights are the checkpoint at the end of pre-training, before any mid- or post-training, and can serve as a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research.
To be worth building on, a base model has to stay affordable to train and run, so efficiency was a design goal from the outset. Further training samples from the model repeatedly, and agentic applications bring multi-turn interactions and long contexts. Both add to compute and memory costs. ERNIE 5.5 Flash therefore revisits the trade-off between capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, and weighs activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost together rather than one at a time.
The same thinking shaped the data and the training system. Every later stage of training builds on what pre-training provides, so the corpus emphasizes capabilities that are hard to add afterwards, such as repository-scale code and long-context understanding. And because an efficient architecture pays off only if it can also be trained efficiently at scale, we designed the model and the training system together.
We hope this release spares more developers the cost of large-scale pre-training, so they can spend their own resources on the capabilities, tasks and training methods they care about.
Key highlights:
An open starting point for further training.
Base weights with no mid- or post-training, leaving the community free to pursue its own approaches to domain adaptation, reasoning and agent training.
Built for efficient further training and inference.
Sparse MoE and hybrid sparse attention balance model capacity, activated compute and long-context cost in the architecture itself.
Broad data, efficient training.
Diverse, high-quality pre-training data gives later training a well-rounded foundation, and a training system co-designed with the architecture keeps large-scale pre-training efficient.
A clean research baseline.
A single checkpoint taken at the end of pre-training makes it easy to compare training methods under controlled conditions and to measure what each one adds.
2. Model Architecture
ERNIE 5.5 Flash model architecture
Click to view full image ↗
ERNIE 5.5 Flash has 43 Transformer layers, a hidden size of 4096 and 64 attention heads.
2.1 Latent-Gated Sparse Attention
Hybrid MLA + HCA attention:
Most layers need only a coarse view of the distant past, so only one layer in seven keeps token-level access to the full context, using Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). The remaining layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA): each compresses every 128 tokens into a single cached entry, then attends to all of these entries plus a short window of recent, uncompressed tokens. An HCA layer therefore still sees the whole sequence, while caching only a small fraction of what a full-context layer needs.
Layer-specific head dimensions:
Instead of using the same head dimension in every layer, we set it according to how expensive each layer's attention is: cheap layers get wide heads, expensive layers get narrower ones. HCA layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, so their attention is cheap and they can afford wide 512-dim heads at little extra compute. MLA layers attend at token level and cost more, so they use narrower 256-dim heads for both query/key and value.
Concentrating the KV-cache budget on MLA layers:
With HCA in most layers, the main question is where to spend the rest of the KV-cache budget. One option is many Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) layers, which compress the history 4× and attend only to a selected part of it. We instead use a few MLA layers that keep every token. In our pre-training comparisons at a similar KV-cache budget, HCA combined with MLA outperforms HCA combined with CSA.
Sparse attention in the full-context layers:
The MLA layers are the only layers that see every distant token individually. With dense attention, they would account for most of the attention compute at long context lengths, so they use sparse attention (DSA) instead. A lightweight indexer scores past positions for each query, and core attention is computed only over the top-k highest-scoring positions. The per-query cost of core attention therefore stays constant as the context grows. With DSA, these layers match dense attention in pre-training loss and train substantially faster.
Two further changes apply inside the attention layers:
Low-Rank Gated Attention:
Gated attention multiplies the attention output by a learned gate, which has been shown to improve both quality and training stability. Normally the gate is computed from the layer's hidden state. We instead compute it from the low-rank query latent, a compressed form of the query that each attention layer already computes. Because this latent is 4× narrower than the hidden state, the gate projection has 75% fewer weights, and our ablations also show better performance. Every attention layer in ERNIE 5.5 Flash, MLA and HCA alike, uses Low-Rank Gated Attention.
Virtual Head Attention (VHA)
:
After attention, VHA adds a lightweight low-rank mixing step across heads, with an identity skip connection. This lets heads share information, which improves expressiveness and training quality, and at inference it is fused into the attention kernel with negligible overhead.
2.2 Multi-Router Latent MoE
A conventional MoE layer picks experts with a single router and a hard top-k. We find that
a single router's scores correlate only weakly with how useful each expert actually is, especially in the middle and deeper layers
. And because experts left out of the top-k receive no gradient from that token, the router gets no signal that it chose wrongly, so wrong selections tend to reinforce themselves.
Multi-Router
replaces the single router with several independently initialized sigmoid routers that score the experts jointly.
The routers develop clearly distinct preferences
: an expert can be chosen because one router strongly favors it or because several favor it together, so a wrong choice is easier to correct. The errors of any one router no longer decide the selection, and routing becomes less sensitive to noisy features and distribution shift. The number of activated experts, expert FLOPs and communication volume stay the same. Compared with a single router,
routing scores correlate noticeably better with how useful each expert is
, with the largest gains in the middle and deeper layers.
All layers except the first use an MoE feed-forward block:
512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert
, with auxiliary-loss-free, bias-corrected load balancing.
Latent experts.
Each MoE layer first projects tokens from 4096 to a 2048-d latent space; the experts (intermediate size 2048) run in that space, and a single shared up-projection maps the result back to 4096. This roughly halves dispatch/combine traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts.
Stable LatentMoE design with learnable scalars.
The MoE blocks follow the Stable LatentMoE design (an RMSNorm before the up-projection and SiTU-GLU expert activations), which keeps expert outputs well scaled across all 43 layers and stabilizes optimization. In addition, each routed expert's routing weight is multiplied by its own learnable scalar.
2.3 Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)
ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the standard residual connection with mHC: each layer reads from and writes to 4 parallel residual streams through a constrained mixing matrix, which gives layers a wider channel for passing information to one another at negligible extra compute.
2.4 MultiMax Output Head
A single softmax temperature forces a trade-off: lowering it makes the distribution sparse but also suppresses other plausible tokens; raising it keeps them but fattens the long tail of implausible ones. MultiMax replaces the single temperature with a learnable piecewise temperature, so the output head no longer has to choose: it suppresses the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping several plausible next tokens. The logits are rescaled element-wise inside the chunked, Triton-fused cross-entropy kernel just before the softmax. This adds negligible training overhead and no extra memory, and significantly lowers pre-training loss.
2.5 ECHO: Replacing the MTP Module
Conventional multi-token prediction (MTP) attaches extra modules to the backbone to predict future tokens, so the loss on future tokens mostly trains those modules, and the backbone is still trained mainly to predict the next token. ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the MTP module with
ECHO
, which
reuses the backbone's own final layer
to predict future tokens. Because there is no separate MTP layer, the loss on future tokens directly trains the same parameters that produce the next token. Learning to look past the next token encourages the backbone to anticipate where the sequence is heading, with clear gains on reasoning and code. ERNIE 5.5 Flash is pre-trained with single-step ECHO. The same layer also serves as the draft model for speculative decoding, and it generalizes beyond its training: although trained to predict only one extra token, it drafts several tokens ahead, with a higher acceptance rate than an auxiliary MTP module trained the same way.
2.6 Tokenizer
ERNIE 5.5 Flash uses a new BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of about 200K entries. Numbers are tokenized
right-to-left (R2L) in groups of up to three digits
, so that digits with the same place value line up across numbers of different lengths (e.g. 1,234,567 →
1
234
567
). This helps with arithmetic and number-heavy text.
3. Pre-training
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base was pre-trained from scratch on
33.5T tokens
with the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to
128K tokens
over the course of pre-training, and fine-tuning and inference support a
1M-token
context. The released checkpoint is taken at the end of pre-training and has not gone through any mid-training or post-training.
3.1 Data
The pre-training corpus covers a wide range of domains and languages and is curated for both breadth of knowledge and quality. Beyond this broad base, we focused on three areas:
Web data.
Multilingual web data is crawled at scale, extracted with high fidelity and filtered by models that score quality along several dimensions. The result covers a broad range of knowledge and is dense in useful training signal.
Code data.
Code collected from repositories and the web is filtered to remove non-code content, aggressively deduplicated and graded for quality at several granularities. Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
The sci-fi anthology, titled Gods Don’t Give Gifts, releases in December.

Andrew Webster
is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.
The AI-generated sci-fi film
Gods Don’t Give Gifts
has added a bit of star power: Pop star Grimes is going to appear in the movie. Billed as “the first AI film to come to theatres,”
Gods Don’t Give Gifts
is a notable test case for the commercial potential of AI films, and it releases on December 4th. Grimes — who will be lending both her likeness and vocal performance to the movie, which you can see in the clip above — potentially gives the project some legitimacy.
AI studio Fable, which is producing the film, claimed in a press release that “casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films.”
Gods Don’t Give Gifts
is being directed by Jack London, better known under the online handle
Gossip Goblin
.
Related
The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
Gods Don’t Give Gifts
is an anthology that’s set in a future “where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized” and depicts what happens when “four interconnected stories collide with the horrifying consequences of humanity’s attempt to transcend the flesh.” Those themes seem to fit pretty snugly with Grimes’ interests, as she has explored themes of transhumanism and artificial intelligence in the past. It’s also not the only AI project she’s working on, with
an AI-themed album called
Psy Opera
in the works
.
Here’s the trailer for
Gods Don’t Give Gifts
:
While there has been
plenty of hype around the potential for AI in Hollywood
, there’s yet to be a project that shows that the technology is actually a vital storytelling tool. Previous examples, like two different takes on
The Odyssey
—
including one made with Elon Musk’s Grok
—
have left plenty to be desired
.
